title: How vulnerable are our smart devices?
description:
More and more of our tech is connected to the internet. Maybe you're wearing a fitness tracker right now, or you've got a smart doorbell, speaker or lamp at home.

So what happens when those devices get hacked? And is there anything you can do to protect them?

You might remember that in October, supermarkets across Europe were hit by a major cyber hack that caused fridge and freezer systems to heat up. Some stores say that their fridge temperatures rose as high as 50C (122F).

BBC tech reporter Shiona McCallum explains how older, internet-connected refrigeration tech with weak protections and remote management can be exploited, and why the wider risk extends to other connected systems in areas like banking, agriculture and utilities.

Plus cybersecurity educator Joan Nwafor shares tips on how to keep your smart devices safe and secure from cyber hacks.

summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討智慧裝置與連網設備的資安漏洞問題。歐洲多家超市的連網冷凍系統近期遭駭客入侵，導致溫度飆升至 50 度並廢棄大量食物。 BBC 科技記者 Shiona McCallum 表示，許多舊型連網設備僅靠簡易密碼保護，容易遭駭客攻擊，此風險更可能波及金融與農業等基礎設施。英國國家網路安全中心 NCSC 也針對數萬台連網設備進行修補。網路安全教育員 Joan Nwafor 則建議民眾修改預設密碼、定期更新軟體，並將智慧家電連至獨立網路。
summaryEn: In this episode of What in the World, host Hannah Gelbart examines the cybersecurity vulnerabilities of smart devices following a major cyber attack on European supermarkets that pushed fridge and freezer temperatures up to 50°C, resulting in massive food waste. BBC tech reporter Shiona McCallum explains that older connected equipment with weak password security and remote access features can easily be exploited, threatening broader critical sectors like banking, agriculture, and public utilities. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre also intervened to secure tens of thousands of vulnerable refrigeration units across the country. Additionally, cybersecurity educator Joan Nwafor offers practical tips for consumers, advising them to change default passwords, routinely update software, and keep smart home devices on a separate network.
